overview: After 2...exf4 White brings the queen to g4 at once, attacking g7 and the f4 pawn. Black replies with ...Nf6 or ...d5, hitting the queen with tempo, and after Qxf4 White has regained the pawn but has spent time with the queen. Black usually gets a comfortable game with a lead in development.

white_ideas.idea: Regain f4 with the queen after Qg4 and Qxf4
Threaten g7 and use the open f-file
Develop quickly and castle before the queen is harassed

black_ideas.idea: Develop with tempo and take the centre
Avoid pawn grabs that cost time

typical_structures.structure: White queen exposed on f4 or g4, Black pieces developed with tempo

character.notes: Black is happy to develop with tempo against an early queen; a tactical but one-sided opening.

gambit.notes: On the main line 3...Nf6 4.Qxf4 White wins the pawn straight back, so nothing is given up.

soundness.notes: White loses time with the queen and Black gets the better of the opening; poorly regarded.

structure.notes: Open e- and d-files with queens and minor pieces active.

approach.notes: A rare sideline that strong players avoid.

level.notes: Easy to learn but dubious, so it is not a safe repertoire choice.

sublines_that_differ.name: Black grabs g7 or ...d5 lines
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. f4 exf4 3. Qg4 d5
sublines_that_differ.how: Black hits the queen at once and takes the centre.

character.reason: Black develops with tempo and White regains the pawn, so the game is not especially forcing.

gambit.reason: White regains the f4 pawn by force with Qxf4 after ...Nf6, so nothing is given up in the main line.

soundness.reason: Strong players think the early queen loses time against sensible replies.

structure.reason: Open centre with queens and pieces active on the e-file.

approach.reason: Strong players do not choose it.

level.reason: A dubious line cannot be Beginner, though it needs little theory.

plans.reason: White queen is out early; Black develops with tempo.
